title: COVID-19 in Polish-language social media - misinformation vs government information
screen_reason: BuzzSumo study of Polish-language COVID-19 items shared on social media (161,404 items, 41,432,352 engagements, Jan 2020 - Jun 2021). Two medical doctors independently coded the 40 most-engaged items against an evidence-based-medicine textbook and national pharmacotherapy guidelines; 4 of the 40 were classified as misinformation ('manipulated news'), accounting for 244,700 engagements, 7.66% of top-40 engagement. Both a share of shared items and a share of engagement are reported with explicit denominators, so the paper is eligible.

estimates.platform: social media aggregated by BuzzSumo Enterprise - predominantly Facebook, also Twitter, Reddit and Pinterest
estimates.date: January 1, 2020 to June 30, 2021 (Methods and Results; the Abstract instead says 'January 1 to June 30, 2022')
estimates.measure_type: % of the 40 most-engaged Polish-language COVID-19 social media items classified as misinformation
estimates.value_raw: 4 of the top 40 items ('for "Manipulated News," there were 4 instances'; 'Sufficient' 26, 'Irrelevant' 10, fabricated 0, advertisement 0)
estimates.denominator: the 40 Polish-language COVID-19 items with the highest total social-media engagement, drawn from 161,404 items identified by BuzzSumo
estimates.definition: classified as 'Manipulated news' - generally true basic information, but false conclusions or recommendations coming from over-interpreted or overly extrapolated results (all four were manipulated news; none were fabricated news or advertisement news)
estimates.misinfo_def: "misinformation pertains to information that is false but spread unintentionally, without the aim to harm. Due to the challenges in determining whether the dissemination of false information is intentional or accidental, the term 'misinformation' is commonly used to denote any type of false information, irrespective of the intent to cause harm" (WHO definitions adopted)
estimates.source_quote: Among the top 40 items with the most engagements, our analysis indicates a high prevalence of cases classified as "Sufficient." In the "Sufficient" category, there were 26 instances, in the "Irrelevant" category, there were 10 instances, and for "Manipulated News," there were 4 instances. There were '0' fake news and '0' advertisement items (see Supplementary materials).
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Social media engagement', p. 3; Table 2 lists the four items
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two of the authors (PW and EL), both medical doctors, independently assessed each of the top 40 items and assigned them to five categories (fabricated / manipulated / advertisement / irrelevant / sufficient news). Reference standards: the COVID-19 chapter of 'Interna Szczeklika', a Polish evidence-based-medicine textbook, and the official Polish COVID-19 pharmacotherapy guidelines from the Agency for Health Technology Assessment and Tariff System. The Internet Wayback Machine was used to retrieve the original versions of altered or deleted items. Observed agreement 94.12%, Cohen's kappa 0.882 (95% CI 0.782-0.982); disagreements reevaluated to consensus.
estimates.moderator_quote: We examined Polish-language items on social media from January 1, 2020, to June 30, 2021 ... The keywords employed were "COVID" OR "koronawirus" OR "SARS-CoV-2". BuzzSumo not only facilitates a comprehensive overview of the query but also furnishes a ranking of the top shared stories. For qualitative analysis, our focus was on the top 40 items that garnered the highest total engagement on social media.
estimates.notes: 10.0% is 4/40, both numbers verbatim, same denominator (R8-compliant). The paper never states 10% itself; its Abstract says 'Four items classified as misinformation accounted for 7.7 % of the Top 40 items', which mislabels the ENGAGEMENT share (7.66%) as an item share - an internal error worth flagging. denom_selection=curated: only the 40 most-engaged items were coded, so this is the misinformation rate among the most-shared COVID items, not among Polish COVID content generally. Coded SHARING rather than CONTENT because the corpus is items ranked by social-media engagement (shared links), per the rule that '% of shared links unreliable' is SHARING. breadth=misleading: the paper explicitly found zero fabricated items; all four were over-interpretation of real findings. Date conflict between Abstract (2022) and Methods/Results (2020-2021) - Methods/Results used.

estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same coding as the item-share row: two author medical doctors, independent classification against 'Interna Szczeklika' and Polish COVID-19 pharmacotherapy guidelines; observed agreement 94.12%, kappa 0.882 (95% CI 0.782-0.982).
estimates.moderator_quote: By the end of the study period (June 30, 2021), the top 40 shared COVID-19 items had amassed 3194,900 engagements, constituting 7.71 % of the total.
estimates.notes: Engagement-weighted counterpart of the item-share row (same country x platform x definition cell, different measure, so a separate row). unit coded 'exposure' because the denominator counts engagements, not items - there is no 'engagement' option in the unit vocabulary. Value stated verbatim (7.66%). Denominator is again restricted to the coded top 40, not the whole corpus.

missed_or_uncertain: DELIBERATELY NOT EXTRACTED, with reasons an adjudicator may want to overturn: (1) 'manipulated news items ... make up a minuscule percentage of the total COVID-19 items (only 0.002 %)' and 'receive ... 0.591 % of total engagement'. Both are stated verbatim (4/161,404 items; 244,700/41,432,352 engagements), but the numerator comes only from the 40 items that were actually coded while the denominator is the entire uncoded corpus. Any misinformation among the other 161,364 items is uncounted, so these are strict LOWER BOUNDS, not prevalence estimates, and pooling them would bias a prevalence synthesis downward by orders of magnitude. If the review wants them, they should be flagged borderline and never pooled. (2) 'The top 40 items (0.02 % of all items) accounted for 7.71 % of engagements (3,194,900)' - a genuine concentration statement (top 0.025% of items -> 7.711% of engagement), but the concentrated group is ITEMS rather than users or sources (conc_unit admits only user|source) and the concentration is of engagement with ALL COVID content, not with misinformation, so it falls outside the review's CONCENTRATION construct. Flagged here in case the review defines concentration more broadly. (3) Government-source engagement shares (gov.pl = 0.9% of overall engagement, 4.09% of top-40 engagement) - not misinformation. (4) Facebook reaction distributions ('haha' 40% of general items, 58% of gov.pl items; 'angry' and 'love' each 42.5% of top-40 reactions) - reaction composition, not misinformation prevalence. (5) All comparison figures the paper quotes from other studies, forbidden by the cite-from-elsewhere rule: the authors' own 2018 Polish study ('up to 40 % of the most frequently shared health information was classified as misinformation'; vaccines '9 out of 10 items'), the Italian BuzzSumo study (misinformation '23.1 % of the total shares'), 'median percentage of misclassified news was 25 %', the Rutgers Facebook study ('32 % of the articles were accurate, 18 % were incorrect, and 50 % were misleading', 6.61M vs 2.2M shares), and the Polish vaccination-comment study (4042/18,685 comments, with its category percentages). TEXT ISSUE: the Abstract's data window ('January 1 to June 30, 2022') contradicts the Methods and Results ('January 1, 2020, to June 30, 2021'); the latter is corroborated by Table 2's item dates (Mar-Oct 2020) and by Fig. 1, so 2020-2021 was used. The Abstract also reports the item count as 0.02% while the Results give 0.025%.

rob.design: Cross-sectional content analysis of the most-engaged items in a BuzzSumo Enterprise query. Frame: all Polish-language social-media items matching 'COVID' OR 'koronawirus' OR 'SARS-CoV-2', 1 Jan 2020 - 30 Jun 2021 (161,404 items, 41,432,352 engagements); only the 40 items with the highest total engagement were coded, so the qualitative sample is rank-truncated and not representative. No response rate (platform data). Coding: two author medical doctors independently classified each item into five predefined categories carried over from the team's earlier study, using the Polish EBM textbook 'Interna Szczeklika' (COVID-19 chapter) and official national COVID-19 pharmacotherapy guidelines as the reference standard; the Wayback Machine was used to recover original versions of edited or deleted items. Reliability reported: observed agreement 94.12%, Cohen's kappa 0.882 (95% CI 0.782-0.982), disagreements reevaluated to consensus. Analysis descriptive (Excel). Item-level data in Supplementary materials.
